# Affect: states that last {#sec-affect}

<div data-life="status" data-stage="1.8"></div>

Everything this brain does so far, it does about the present. A bush is in front of it, so it bites. The skin is
cold, so it walks. The stomach is empty, so it forages. When the cause is gone, the behaviour is gone in the same
moment.

But some events say something about the minutes that follow. An animal that has just eaten well is probably
standing in a good place. An animal that has just been hurt is probably standing in a bad one. To use that, the
brain has to keep something of the event after it is over. This stage adds two such states: an alarm after pain,
and contentment after a meal. So that the states have something to work with, the bushes in this world grow in
patches of one kind each.

<div data-life="brain" data-stage="1.8"></div>

## The circuit

Two *modulators*, substances that a few cells release and that reach many cells at once, each released by one
event and cleared slowly. And three new cells.

- **Alarm.** Pain releases the modulator `alarm`. It drives a new cell, **`flee`**, which pushes the animal
  forward. After a poison bite the animal keeps going for a short while, out of the patch of poison.
- **Serotonin.** A new cell, **`fed`**, fires when the animal tastes food, and releases the modulator `serotonin`.
  It drives a new cell, **`settle`**, which switches on `rest`, the cell of the previous stage that holds the
  forward step back. After a meal the animal stays where it ate, also where it is cold.

`hungry` still shuts `rest`, as before. So a fed animal stays in the good patch until it is hungry again, and then
it forages, with good bushes close by.

The two states are not a second system next to the drives. They act on the same cells: the drives decide what the
animal does from what the body needs now, and the two modulators push those same modes for a while after an event.

The wiring is designed. Evolution may tune every strength, and also how fast each modulator is cleared, which
sets how long each state lasts.

## The biology: affect

A drive, as in the previous stage, follows the body: the hunger cell fires for as long as the stomach is empty and
stops when it is full. An *affective state* is different in one respect. Something sets it off, and then it stays
for a while by itself, after its cause has gone.

In small animals such states are carried by *neuromodulators*. They are released quickly and cleared slowly, and
that slowness is the memory. The roundworm *C. elegans* slows down and stays where it is for minutes after it has
found food, under the influence of serotonin. After a harmful touch it speeds away, and keeps going well after
the touch has ended.

Such a state has two sides. It is good or bad, and it makes the animal more active or less. An animal that is
alarmed is in a bad and active state. An animal that is content is in a good and quiet one.

## The world: every kind of bush in its own patches

In the world of the previous stage the bushes of every kind were spread evenly. There, a meal says nothing about
the place: the bush that was just emptied stays empty for a long time, and what grows next to it is as likely to
be poison as anywhere else. A state that lasts has nothing to work with.

So the bushes now grow in patches, and every patch holds one kind. After a good meal, the neighbouring bushes are
most likely good as well. After a poison bite, the neighbours are most likely poison too. What just happened says
what is near.

The rest is as before: the world is cold, the hot springs are spread evenly, and the four kinds of berry bush are
new in every life, half of them poison.

<div data-life="settings" data-stage="1.8"></div>

## Results

### Main against control

The control is the brain of the previous stage in this world of patches. It feels pain and tastes food as before,
but nothing of either stays with it.

<div data-life="curves" data-stage="1.8"></div>

<div data-life="summary" data-stage="1.8"></div>

The animals with the two states do better than the control in every seed, and by about the same amount in each.
Unlike in the previous stage, the rows of the table agree. Sharing a world with control animals, the animals of
this stage also come out ahead: staying in a good patch keeps an animal next to its next meal, and that helps in a
race for berries as much as it does among its own kind.

Both populations were still improving when the runs ended. The control improves too: without any lasting state,
evolution makes it rest more, which keeps some of the animals near where they ate.

### Is the circuit used?

<div data-life="lesions" data-stage="1.8"></div>

Both new states are used. Silencing `fed` or `settle` gives nearly the same result, because they form one chain:
without either, a meal leaves no serotonin behind and the animal no longer stays. Silencing `flee` costs less.
The alarm is short and acts only after a poison bite, which is a small part of a life.

Two things from earlier stages have lost their use in this world.

- Silencing `cold` or `warm_seek` no longer costs anything. In the previous stage a fed animal walked while it was
  cold, until it found warmth. Here that walk takes it out of a good patch, and staying where the food is turns
  out to be worth more than being warm.
- Switching the learning off costs little. In a patch of one kind, the first bite tells the animal what it needs
  to know about all the bushes around it, and the alarm carries it away from them. Knowing a poison by its look
  matters less when poison no longer stands between the good bushes.

Neither was removed. The cells are part of the previous stages as they were frozen, and a later world may need
them again.

### After a bite

<div data-life="table" data-stage="1.8" data-example="after_a_bite"></div>

The two states can be seen in what the animals do in the twenty ticks after a bite. After a poison bite the
animals of this stage take more steps than the control. After a good meal they take almost none.

### How a life is spent

<div data-life="table" data-stage="1.8" data-example="life_spent"></div>

Both populations stand still for most of their life. Much of that time they bite at nothing: an animal that is held
in place by `rest` still has its grasp programme, and a bite costs little.
